name: Commando -- POKEY music player
note: The same engine as Midnight Mutants, on a different chip.
That is not a guess from the sound of it. The two players lay their
tables out in the same order and the same shapes: a 16-entry duration
table, then 16 instrument records of 16 bytes each with only the first
ten used, then pointer lists ended by an entry whose high byte is zero,
then count-prefixed patterns of fixed-size notes. Midnight Mutants keeps
its durations at f6:$7734 and its instruments at f6:$7744, sixteen bytes
apart; Commando keeps them at b6:$A941 and b6:$A951, sixteen bytes apart.
Atari-era houses shared their sound code, and this is what that looks
like from the ROM side.
Checked against the machine, not just against itself. A 45-second
capture of the cartridge running in the emulator matches song 0 on
576 of 576 frames across all four voices -- every AUDC, AUDF and
volume, every frame. Song 1 follows it in the same capture and matches
94 of its 96 frames; the last two are the player cutting the final note
short to start what comes next, which is sequencing above the level a
song describes. A no-op push of all 43 patterns changes zero bytes.
What differs is forced by the chip. TIA's AUDF is five bits, so Midnight
Mutants has three bits spare in the pitch byte and spends them on an
index into a waveform table. POKEY's AUDF is the whole byte, so there is
no room, and the control value comes from the instrument instead --
`audc_from: instrument` selects that. Same idea, different budget.
_audc_from: Where a note's AUDC comes from. `instrument` takes it from the high
nibble of the instrument's first byte, which is also the byte the
envelope ORs its volume into -- one byte carrying distortion and volume,
which is exactly POKEY's AUDC register.

titles.3: victory, when a level is cleared
titles.4: extended victory fanfare, possibly the game-win -- unconfirmed

_titles: Identified by playing the game and listening -- there is nothing in the
bytes that says which tune is the title theme, and no analysis recovers
it. Song 4 is the one guess in the list: it is clearly an extended
arrangement of song 3's victory theme, and where it plays is unconfirmed.
It is not a remix of song 3 in the literal sense, which is worth saying
because it sounds like one: the two share no pattern bytes, their
longest identical run of pitches is four notes, and the seven pitches
they have in common are simply the key. The resemblance is the same
instrument palette and the same scale over different music.
The rest were placed by ear against the running cartridge. Songs 5 to 8
and 10 are background music without a more specific role established.
_banks: Every table this player uses -- durations, instruments, tracks and
patterns -- sits in bank 6, so every song resolves there. Midnight
Mutants spreads its songs across banks and has to say which; this one
keeps the whole engine and all its music in one, but the pointers are
still in the paged window and so the bank still has to be named.
_voice_ptr: Four voices, so four pointers per song. Songs that use fewer leave the
unused slots zero -- songs 1 and 2 are two-voice and read as such.

_no_waveform: There is no waveform field: the pitch byte is all eight bits of AUDF.
Confirmed rather than assumed -- pitches across every pattern span
$00 to $F3, so nothing above bit 4 is free to hold anything else.

_note: longest first, so the note's duration nibble is an index and not a
length. It sits immediately before the instruments, as in Midnight

_engine: The same five-stage envelope: attack, decay, sustain, release, off,
with volume as an 8-bit accumulator whose high nibble reaches the
4-bit volume field. Ten of the sixteen bytes in a row are read, and
the other six are zero in every row here -- which is itself evidence
that the record was sized for this engine and not trimmed for POKEY.
